chapter.name: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions

questions.q: Every sip from a glass of homemade ORS tastes equally sweet and equally salty, from the first sip to the last. What does this tell us about the ORS?
questions.a: The sugar and salt are evenly distributed throughout the water, so the ORS is a uniform mixture.
o: The sugar and salt are evenly distributed in the water, so it is a uniform mixture
The sugar and salt have settled at the bottom, so it is a non-uniform mixture
The sugar and salt have turned into water, so only water is left in the glass
The water has dissolved in the sugar, so sugar is the solvent in ORS

questions.q: To make a skin lotion, a pharmacist mixes 20 mL of glycerine with 80 mL of rose water. The two liquids mix evenly. Which is the solute in this solution?
questions.a: Glycerine, because in a solution of two liquids the one present in the smaller amount is the solute.
o: Glycerine, because it is present in the smaller amount
Rose water, because it is present in the larger amount
Glycerine, because it is the thicker of the two liquids
Neither, because two liquids cannot form a solution

questions.q:
Match each term in Column I with its meaning in Column II.
Column I: 1. Solution  2. Solute  3. Solvent  4. Non-uniform mixture
Column II: P. The liquid in which a solid dissolves  Q. A mixture whose components can be seen with the naked eye or a magnifying device  R. A uniform mixture whose components are not seen separately  S. The solid that dissolves in a liquid
True or false? 'When a solution is made by mixing two liquids, the liquid that is poured in last is the solute.' Give your verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The order of pouring does not decide it. When two liquids form a solution, the liquid present in the smaller amount is the solute and the one present in the larger amount is the solvent.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: the liquid present in the smaller amount is the solute, whatever the order of pouring

questions.q:
Answer each part in one line.
(a) What is a solution?
(b) Common salt is stirred into water until it disappears. Name the solute.
(c) In the same salt water, name the solvent.
(d) 30 mL of liquid A is mixed evenly with 70 mL of liquid B. Which liquid is the solute?
(e) Sand is stirred into water and soon settles at the bottom. Is this mixture a solution? Give one reason.
questions.a: (a) A solution is a uniform mixture in which the components are evenly distributed. (b) Salt. (c) Water. (d) Liquid A, because it is present in the smaller amount. (e) No. The sand can be seen separately and settles, so the components are not evenly distributed: it is a non-uniform mixture.
s: (a) Defines a solution as a uniform mixture with the components evenly distributed
(b) Names salt as the solute
(c) Names water as the solvent
(d) Names liquid A, the smaller amount, as the solute
(e) Says no, because the sand is seen separately (non-uniform mixture)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A mixture of sand and water is not a solution.
Reason (R): Sand is a solid.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Salt is also a solid, yet it forms a solution with water; sand and water is not a solution because the sand is not evenly distributed and can be seen separately.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: To make a hand rub, a pharmacist mixes 0.4 L of surgical spirit with 350 mL of water. The two liquids mix evenly into a clear liquid. Which one is the solute?
questions.a: Water, because 350 mL is less than 0.4 L (which is 400 mL), and in a solution of two liquids the smaller amount is the solute.
o: Water, because 350 mL is less than 0.4 L, which is 400 mL
Surgical spirit, because 0.4 is a smaller number than 350
Surgical spirit, because water is always the solvent
Neither, because the solute in a solution must be a solid

questions.q:
The science club of a school in Nashik sets up four beakers for a display.
Beaker 1: 300 g of sugar stirred into 100 g of hot water; the syrup is clear and equally sweet everywhere.
Beaker 2: chalk powder stirred into water; white particles settle at the bottom after some time.
Beaker 3: 60 mL of vinegar mixed with 140 mL of water; the liquid is clear and even throughout.
Beaker 4: sawdust stirred into water; the sawdust floats on top.
(a) Which two beakers hold solutions? Give the evidence from the description.
(b) Name the solute and the solvent in Beaker 1.
(c) Name the solute in Beaker 3, and say how you decided.
(d) A visitor says, 'The solute is always the part present in the smaller amount.' Which one beaker would you use to show that this is not always true, and why?
questions.a: (a) Beakers 1 and 3: each is clear and the same throughout, so the components are evenly distributed; in Beakers 2 and 4 the chalk and sawdust can be seen separately. (b) Sugar is the solute and water is the solvent. (c) Vinegar, because both are liquids and the one present in the smaller amount (60 mL against 140 mL) is the solute. (d) Beaker 1: there is more sugar (300 g) than water (100 g), yet sugar is the solute, because when a solid dissolves in a liquid the solid is always the solute, whatever the amounts.
s: (a) Picks Beakers 1 and 3, because they are uniform (same throughout)
(b) Sugar is the solute and water is the solvent
(c) Vinegar, the smaller of the two liquids, is the solute
(d) Chooses Beaker 1: more sugar than water, yet the solid is the solute by the solid-in-liquid rule

questions.q: Juhi says, 'Water is always the solvent in any solution made with water.' Test her claim on these two solutions: (i) 250 g of sugar dissolved in 100 g of water to make a syrup; (ii) 200 mL of a clear liquid mixed evenly with 50 mL of water. For which solution does her claim hold, and for which does it fail? How should she correct her statement?
questions.a: (i) Her claim holds: water is the solvent even though there is more sugar, because when a solid dissolves in a liquid, the liquid is always the solvent. (ii) Her claim fails: both are liquids, so the one in the smaller amount is the solute, and 50 mL of water is less than 200 mL, so water is the solute here. Correction: water is always the solvent when a solid dissolves in it, but when two liquids mix, the liquid in the larger amount is the solvent, which may not be water.
s: (i) Claim holds: water is the solvent by the solid-in-liquid rule, whatever the amounts
(ii) Claim fails: water (50 mL) is the smaller liquid, so it is the solute
Corrects the statement: water is always the solvent for a solid; for two liquids the larger amount is the solvent

questions.q: A lab assistant mixes 0.15 L of liquid P with 120 mL of liquid Q, and they mix evenly. (a) Which liquid is the solute? (b) She then stirs in another 40 mL of liquid Q. Which liquid is the solute now? Show the comparison.
questions.a: (a) 0.15 L = 150 mL, and 120 mL is less than 150 mL, so Q is the solute. (b) Q is now 120 + 40 = 160 mL, which is more than 150 mL of P, so P is now the solute.
s: (a) Converts 0.15 L to 150 mL and names Q (120 mL) as the solute
(b) Finds Q = 160 mL, more than 150 mL, and names P as the solute now

questions.q: What is a solution called in which more solute can still be dissolved at the given temperature?
questions.a: An unsaturated solution.

questions.q: Glass X has 3 spoons of sugar dissolved in 150 mL of water. Glass Y has 3 spoons of the same sugar dissolved in 300 mL of water. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Glass X is more concentrated than glass Y, since the same amount of sugar is in less water.
o: Glass X is more concentrated than glass Y
Glass Y is more concentrated, because it has more water
Both are equally concentrated, because each has 3 spoons of sugar
Glass X is saturated and glass Y is unsaturated

questions.q: (a) What is meant by the concentration of a solution? (b) Solution M has 10 g of salt dissolved in 100 mL of water and solution N has 25 g of salt dissolved in 100 mL of water. Which one is dilute compared with the other?
questions.a: (a) Concentration is the amount of solute present in a fixed quantity of the solution (or solvent). (b) Solution M is dilute compared with N, because it has less salt in the same 100 mL of water.
s: (a) Concentration: amount of solute in a fixed quantity of solution or solvent
(b) Names M as the dilute one, with less salt in the same amount of water

questions.q: True or false? 'Dilute and concentrated are relative terms, so the same solution can be called dilute when it is compared with one solution and concentrated when it is compared with another.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. A solution is called dilute or concentrated only in comparison: a glass with 2 spoons of salt is dilute compared with a glass of the same water holding 3 spoons, but concentrated compared with one holding 1 spoon.
s: States the verdict: True
Explains that the terms only compare solutions, with an example of one solution being both

questions.q: Rhea adds sugar to 200 mL of water at room temperature, one spoon at a time, stirring well each time. Spoons 1 to 8 dissolve completely, but part of spoon 9 stays at the bottom however long she stirs. (a) After spoon 4, was the solution saturated or unsaturated? (b) What is the solution called once sugar stays undissolved at the bottom? (c) Name the term for the largest amount of sugar that this water can dissolve at this temperature.
questions.a: (a) Unsaturated, because more sugar could still dissolve in it. (b) A saturated solution at that temperature. (c) Solubility.
s: (a) Unsaturated, since more sugar still dissolved after spoon 4
(b) Saturated solution (at that temperature)
(c) Solubility

questions.q: A nurse prepares four salt solutions for gargling. A: 6 g of salt in 250 mL of water. B: 4.5 g in 150 mL. C: 8 g in 400 mL. D: 3.4 g in 120 mL. Which solution is the most concentrated?
questions.a: B, 4.5 g in 150 mL, which is 3 g of salt per 100 mL (A has 2.4 g, C 2 g and D about 2.8 g per 100 mL).

questions.q:
Read these statements about a salt solution kept at one fixed temperature.
I. If solid salt stays at the bottom even after long stirring, the solution above it is saturated.
II. The concentration of a solution is the amount of solute present in a fixed quantity of the solution or solvent.
III. A solution that is called concentrated must also be saturated.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q:
At room temperature, 100 mL of water can dissolve at most 20 g of a solid S (an illustrative value). Ravi has two beakers at this temperature. Beaker P: 13 g of S fully dissolved in 100 mL of water. Beaker R: 45 g of S fully dissolved in 250 mL of water.
(a) Is P saturated or unsaturated? Give a reason.
(b) How many more grams of S can P dissolve at this temperature?
(c) What is the largest mass of S that 250 mL of water can dissolve at this temperature?
(d) How many more grams of S must be dissolved in R to make it saturated?
questions.a: (a) Unsaturated, because 13 g is less than the 20 g that 100 mL can hold. (b) 20 - 13 = 7 g. (c) 250 mL is 2.5 times 100 mL, so 20 x 2.5 = 50 g. (d) 50 - 45 = 5 g.
s: (a) P is unsaturated, as 13 g is below 20 g
(b) Finds 7 g more
(c) Scales to 250 mL: 50 g
(d) Finds 5 g more for R

questions.q:
A paneer dairy in Anand keeps three brine tanks at the same room temperature.
Tank 1: 50 L of water with 9 kg of salt fully dissolved; when a worker adds one more handful of salt, it also dissolves.
Tank 2: 45 L of water to which salt was added until a layer of salt stayed undissolved at the bottom, even after long stirring.
Tank 3: 30 L of water with 6.6 kg of salt fully dissolved.
(a) Which tank holds a saturated solution? Give the evidence.
(b) Is Tank 1 saturated or unsaturated? How do you know?
(c) Find the salt per litre of water in Tank 1 and in Tank 3. Which of the two is more concentrated?
(d) For one batch the dairy needs the most concentrated brine it can make at this temperature. From which tank should it take the clear liquid, and why?
questions.a: (a) Tank 2, because salt stays undissolved at the bottom even after long stirring, so no more can dissolve. (b) Unsaturated, because the extra handful of salt still dissolved. (c) Tank 1: 9 / 50 = 0.18 kg per litre; Tank 3: 6.6 / 30 = 0.22 kg per litre, so Tank 3 is more concentrated. (d) Tank 2: a saturated solution holds the maximum amount of salt that this water can dissolve at this temperature, so its clear liquid is more concentrated than the unsaturated brine of Tanks 1 and 3.
s: (a) Tank 2, with undissolved salt left at the bottom
(b) Tank 1 is unsaturated, as the extra salt dissolved
(c) Finds 0.18 and 0.22 kg per litre and names Tank 3
(d) Chooses Tank 2, because a saturated solution holds the most salt at that temperature

questions.q:
Three students test how much of a salt Z dissolves in water at 25 °C (illustrative values).
Asha: 50 mL of water; after 17.5 g had dissolved, any extra Z stayed at the bottom.
Biju: 200 mL of water; 60 g dissolved completely, and a further 5 g also dissolved.
Chitra: 80 mL of water; she added 30 g, and 2 g stayed undissolved at the bottom.
(a) Using Asha's result, find the solubility of Z in grams per 100 mL of water at 25 °C.
(b) How much Z dissolved in Chitra's water? Find her value per 100 mL of water.
(c) Biju did not test whether even more Z would dissolve. What does his result alone tell us about the solubility of Z?
(d) Do the three results agree with one another? Justify.
(e) Predict the mass of Z needed to make 250 mL of water just saturated at 25 °C.
questions.a: (a) 17.5 g in 50 mL means 35 g per 100 mL. (b) 30 - 2 = 28 g dissolved in 80 mL, which is 28 / 80 x 100 = 35 g per 100 mL. (c) It tells us only that 200 mL can dissolve at least 65 g, so the solubility is at least 32.5 g per 100 mL; it does not give the exact value. (d) Yes. Asha and Chitra both give 35 g per 100 mL, and Biju's 65 g is not more than the 70 g that 200 mL could hold at 35 g per 100 mL, so his result fits too. (e) 35 x 2.5 = 87.5 g.
s: (a) Finds 35 g per 100 mL from Asha's data
(b) Finds 28 g dissolved and 35 g per 100 mL for Chitra
(c) Solubility is at least 32.5 g per 100 mL; Biju's result gives no exact value
(d) Decides the results agree, checking Biju's 65 g against 70 g
(e) Predicts 87.5 g for 250 mL

questions.q: For most solid substances, what happens to their solubility in water when the temperature of the water is increased?
questions.a: It increases.
o: It decreases, as it does for gases
It increases only for coloured solids

questions.q: Four samples of the same pond water are kept at different temperatures. Which sample can hold the most dissolved oxygen?
questions.a: The sample at 10 °C, because the solubility of gases in water decreases as temperature increases.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Cold water can provide more oxygen for fish than warm water.
Reason (R): The solubility of gases in water generally decreases as the temperature increases.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) State how the solubility of most solids in water changes as the temperature rises. (b) Give one observation from the baking soda demonstration that supports this.
questions.a: (a) It increases with an increase in temperature. (b) Baking soda that stayed undissolved in water at 20 °C dissolved when the water was heated to 50 °C (and more dissolved again at 70 °C).
s: (a) States that the solubility of most solids increases with temperature
(b) Gives the observation that undissolved baking soda dissolved on heating

questions.q: True or false? 'Warming the water in a fish tank increases the amount of oxygen dissolved in it, just as warming water lets more sugar dissolve.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Gases behave the opposite way to most solids: as water warms up, the solubility of oxygen decreases, so warm water holds less dissolved oxygen.
s: States the verdict: False
Explains that gas solubility decreases as temperature rises, unlike most solids

questions.q: The largest mass of a solid K that dissolves in 100 mL of water is 21 g at 10 °C, 37 g at 30 °C and 46 g at 50 °C (illustrative values). A beaker holds 100 mL of water at 30 °C with 30 g of K fully dissolved. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: It is unsaturated and can dissolve about 7 g more at 30 °C, since 37 - 30 = 7.
o: It is unsaturated and can dissolve about 7 g more at 30 °C
It is saturated, because 30 g is more than 21 g
It is unsaturated and can dissolve 16 g more at 30 °C
It is saturated, because K dissolves fully only at 50 °C

questions.q:
Read these statements about temperature and solubility.
I. A solution that is saturated at 20 °C behaves as an unsaturated solution when it is heated to 50 °C.
II. Since only a little oxygen dissolves in water, it is too little to matter for aquatic life.
III. Water at 70 °C dissolves more baking soda than the same amount of water at 50 °C.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: On a hot day the water in a garden pond warms from 18 °C in the morning to 32 °C in the afternoon. (i) What happens to the amount of oxygen the pond water can hold? (ii) A student suggests pouring hot water into the pond 'so that more oxygen dissolves, the way more sugar dissolves in hot water'. Point out the mistake in this reasoning. (iii) What kind of water would help the fish more, and why?
questions.a: (i) It decreases, because the solubility of oxygen falls as water warms. (ii) The student has used the rule for solids. Gases behave the opposite way: their solubility generally decreases as temperature increases, so hot water would hold even less oxygen. (iii) Cool water, because more oxygen can dissolve in cold water.
s: (i) Oxygen the water can hold decreases as it warms
(ii) Points out that the solid rule was used; gas solubility falls with temperature
(iii) Suggests cool water, which can hold more dissolved oxygen

questions.q:
A small dyeing unit in Sanganer, Jaipur, dissolves a solid dye in water before dipping cloth. Its notebook gives the most dye that 100 L of water can dissolve (illustrative values): at 20 °C, 4 kg; at 40 °C, 7 kg; at 60 °C, 11 kg. For one order, 15 kg of dye must be fully dissolved. After dyeing, the used water, still warm, flows into a nearby stream that has fish.
(a) What is the most dye that 100 L of water can dissolve at 40 °C?
(b) The unit uses a 200 L tank. What is the lowest temperature in the table at which all 15 kg will dissolve? Show the check.
(c) What happens to the dissolved oxygen in the stream near the point where the warm used water enters? Explain.
(d) The owner considers using water at 20 °C in a bigger tank instead. Find the smallest volume of water needed at 20 °C, and give one benefit of this plan for the stream.
questions.a: (a) 7 kg. (b) At 40 °C, 200 L can dissolve 2 x 7 = 14 kg, less than 15 kg; at 60 °C it can dissolve 2 x 11 = 22 kg, which is enough. So the lowest temperature is 60 °C. (c) The warm water raises the stream's temperature, and the solubility of oxygen decreases as water warms, so less oxygen stays dissolved for the fish. (d) At 20 °C each 100 L dissolves 4 kg, so 15 / 4 x 100 = 375 L is needed. The used water would not be warm, so it would not lower the oxygen dissolved in the stream.
s: (a) Reads 7 kg at 40 °C
(b) Checks 14 kg at 40 °C and 22 kg at 60 °C, and chooses 60 °C
(c) Warming lowers the oxygen dissolved in the stream
(d) Finds 375 L and states the benefit: no warm water, so the stream keeps its oxygen

questions.q: A glass of sugar solution at 25 °C has some undissolved sugar at the bottom, even after stirring. It is warmed to 45 °C and stirred, and all the sugar at the bottom dissolves. (a) Was the solution saturated or unsaturated at 25 °C? Give a reason. (b) How could you check whether the warm solution at 45 °C can now dissolve still more sugar?
questions.a: (a) Saturated, because sugar stayed undissolved at the bottom even after stirring. (b) Keep it at 45 °C, add a little more sugar and stir: if it dissolves, the solution is unsaturated at 45 °C; if it stays at the bottom, it is saturated.
s: (a) Saturated at 25 °C, since undissolved sugar remained after stirring
(b) Adds a little more sugar at 45 °C and stirs, reading dissolves = unsaturated, stays = saturated

questions.q: A copper block has a mass of 89 g and a volume of 10 cm³. What is its density?
questions.a: 8.9 g/cm³, since density = mass / volume = 89 / 10.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of density?
questions.a: Kilogram per cubic metre (kg/m³).

questions.q: A jar holds 500 mL of honey with a mass of 710 g. (a) Find the density of the honey in g/mL. (b) Is honey more dense or less dense than water? Use the fact that 1 mL of water has a mass of about 1 g.
questions.a: (a) Density = 710 g / 500 mL = 1.42 g/mL. (b) More dense than water, because 1.42 g/mL is greater than the 1 g/mL of water.
s: (b) Compares with 1 g/mL and says honey is more dense

questions.q: A piece of marble has a mass of 52 g and a volume of 20 cm³. (a) Find its density. (b) Find its relative density with respect to water, taking the density of water as 1 g/cm³. (c) Write the unit of relative density, if it has one.
questions.a: (a) 52 / 20 = 2.6 g/cm³. (b) 2.6 / 1 = 2.6. (c) Relative density has no unit; it is a pure number.
s: (a) Density 2.6 g/cm³
(b) Relative density 2.6
(c) States that relative density has no unit

questions.q: True or false? 'A density of 1 kg/m³ is the same as a density of 1 g/L.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. 1 kg/m³ = 1000 g per 1 m³, and 1 m³ = 1000 L, so it is 1000 g per 1000 L = 1 g/L.
s: States the verdict: True
Shows 1 kg/m³ = 1000 g / 1000 L = 1 g/L

questions.q: A 250 mL bottle of a floor-cleaning liquid holds 300 g of the liquid. Taking the density of water as 1 g/mL, what is the relative density of the cleaning liquid with respect to water?
questions.a: 1.2, a number without units (300 / 250 = 1.2 g/mL, divided by 1 g/mL).

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The relative density of aluminium with respect to water is 2.7 g/cm³.
Reason (R): Relative density of a substance = density of the substance / density of water at that temperature.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. Relative density is one density divided by another, so the units cancel: aluminium's relative density is 2.7, a number without any units.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: Arjun says, 'Two blocks with the same volume must have the same density.' Block X has a volume of 40 cm³ and a mass of 108 g. Block Y has a volume of 40 cm³ and a mass of 316 g. (i) Find the density of each block. (ii) Is Arjun right? (iii) What has his claim left out?
questions.a: (i) X: 108 / 40 = 2.7 g/cm³; Y: 316 / 40 = 7.9 g/cm³. (ii) No, he is wrong: the blocks have the same volume but different densities. (iii) Density is the mass present in a unit volume, so it depends on the mass as well; blocks of different substances pack different masses into the same volume.
s: (i) Finds 2.7 g/cm³ and 7.9 g/cm³
(ii) Verdict: wrong, same volume but different densities
(iii) Explains that density also depends on mass (mass per unit volume), which differs between substances

questions.q:
A workshop must pack one 1 kg block of metal into a box whose inside space is 250 cm³. It has a 1 kg block of aluminium (density 2.7 g/cm³) and a 1 kg block of iron (density 7.9 g/cm³).
(a) Find the volume of the aluminium block, to one decimal place.
(b) Find the volume of the iron block, to one decimal place.
(c) Which block fits in the box?
(d) What mass of aluminium would exactly fill the 250 cm³ space?
(e) The packer says, 'Both blocks are 1 kg, so they must take up the same space.' Explain why this is wrong.
questions.a: (a) Volume = mass / density = 1000 / 2.7 = 370.4 cm³. (b) 1000 / 7.9 = 126.6 cm³. (c) Only the iron block, since 126.6 cm³ is less than 250 cm³ while 370.4 cm³ is more. (d) Mass = density x volume = 2.7 x 250 = 675 g. (e) Equal masses take up equal space only if the densities are equal; iron packs more mass into each cm³ than aluminium, so 1 kg of iron takes up less volume.
s: (a) Finds 370.4 cm³ for aluminium
(b) Finds 126.6 cm³ for iron
(c) Chooses the iron block by comparing with 250 cm³
(d) Finds 675 g of aluminium
(e) Explains that different densities give different volumes for the same mass

questions.q: Four liquids have these densities. P: 1.28 g/mL. Q: 1250 kg/m³. R: 1300 g/L. S: 1.32 g/cm³. Which liquid is the densest? (1 kg/m³ = 1 g/L, and 1 mL = 1 cm³.)
questions.a: S, at 1.32 g/cm³; in the same unit Q is 1.25 g/mL, R is 1.30 g/mL and P is 1.28 g/mL.

questions.q: Which apparatus is used in the laboratory to measure the volume of a liquid?
questions.a: A measuring cylinder.

questions.q: A metal bolt tied to a thread is lowered into a measuring cylinder of water. The water level rises from 30 mL to 38 mL. What is the volume of the bolt?
questions.a: 8 cm³ (38 mL - 30 mL = 8 mL, which is 8 cm³).

questions.q:
Match each quantity in Column I with how it is expressed and found in Column II.
Column I: 1. Mass of a stone  2. Weight of a stone  3. Volume of some milk  4. Volume of a shoe box
Column II: P. In newtons; the force with which the Earth pulls the stone  Q. In grams; read on a balance  R. In mL; read on a measuring cylinder  S. In cm³; found from length x width x height

On a 250 mL measuring cylinder there are 25 small divisions between the 100 mL mark and the 150 mL mark. (a) What volume lies between these two marks? (b) What is the smallest volume that one small division reads?
s: (a) Finds 50 mL between the marks
(b) Divides by 25 divisions to get 2 mL

questions.q:
In the school lab, Tara finds the density of a glass stopper. She switches on a digital weighing balance and it shows 0.000 g. She places a clean watch glass on the pan and the display shows 12.450 g. She presses the tare button and the display returns to 0.000 g. She then places the stopper on the watch glass and the display shows 32.500 g. Next, she fills a 100 mL measuring cylinder with water up to 40 mL, ties the stopper with a thread and lowers it in. The bottom of the meniscus now stands at 53 mL.
(a) What is the mass of the stopper?
(b) Why did Tara press the tare button after placing the watch glass?
(c) What is the volume of the stopper?
(d) Find the density of the glass stopper.
questions.a: (a) 32.500 g. (b) To bring the reading back to zero so that the mass of the watch glass is not counted and the display shows the stopper's mass alone. (c) 53 - 40 = 13 mL, that is 13 cm³. (d) Density = 32.5 / 13 = 2.5 g/cm³.
s: (a) Mass of the stopper is 32.500 g
(b) Taring removes the watch glass's mass from the reading
(c) Volume 53 - 40 = 13 cm³
(d) Density 32.5 / 13 = 2.5 g/cm³

questions.q: Kunal wants the density of some milk. He places an empty beaker on a digital balance and it reads 52.6 g; he forgets to press tare. He measures 40 mL of milk in a measuring cylinder, pours all of it into the beaker, and the balance now reads 93.8 g. (i) Find the mass of the milk. (ii) Find the density of the milk. (iii) Is milk more or less dense than water? Compare using numbers.
questions.a: (i) 93.8 - 52.6 = 41.2 g. (ii) 41.2 g / 40 mL = 1.03 g/mL. (iii) More dense, because 1.03 g/mL is greater than about 1 g/mL for water.
s: (i) Subtracts the beaker: 41.2 g of milk
(ii) Density 41.2 / 40 = 1.03 g/mL
(iii) Compares 1.03 with 1 g/mL and says milk is more dense

questions.q: Pooja writes in her record: 'Using a 100 mL measuring cylinder, I measured 7.35 mL of water in one reading.' (i) What is the smallest volume a 100 mL measuring cylinder usually reads? (ii) Show why her reading cannot have come from this cylinder. (iii) Which size of measuring cylinder would read small volumes like this more finely, and what is its smallest reading?
questions.a: (i) 1 mL. (ii) With 1 mL divisions she can read only whole millilitres, such as 7 mL; a value of 7.35 mL needs a reading to one-hundredth of a millilitre, which this cylinder cannot give. (iii) A 10 mL (or 25 mL) measuring cylinder, whose smallest reading is usually 0.1 mL.
s: (i) States 1 mL for a 100 mL cylinder
(ii) Shows that 7.35 mL needs readings finer than 1 mL divisions
(iii) Names a 10 mL or 25 mL cylinder reading 0.1 mL

questions.q:
Assertion (A): To measure 70 mL of water, a 100 mL measuring cylinder is a better choice than a 500 mL measuring cylinder.
Reason (R): A 500 mL measuring cylinder cannot measure 70 mL of water in one step.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. A 500 mL cylinder can measure 70 mL in one step, but less accurately, since its smallest reading is 5 mL against 1 mL for a 100 mL cylinder.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
A dairy fills buttermilk into 200 mL tetra packs from a cuboid steel tank whose inside measures 1.2 m long, 0.5 m wide and 0.5 m high. The tank is full.
(a) Find the volume of buttermilk in the tank in m³.
(b) Express this volume in litres, using 1 L = 1 dm³ and 1 m³ = 1000 dm³.
(c) How many 200 mL packs can be filled from the tank?
(d) Taking the density of the buttermilk as 1.03 g/mL (an illustrative value), find the mass of buttermilk in the tank in kg.
s: (a) Volume l x w x h = 0.3 m³
(b) Converts to 300 L
(c) Converts to mL and finds 1500 packs

questions.q:
A shop sells a cube-shaped paperweight, each side 3 cm, with a mass of 243 g, and a small figurine of irregular shape with a mass of 81 g. In the lab, the figurine is tied to a thread and lowered into a measuring cylinder; the water level rises from 40 mL to 70 mL.
(a) Find the volume of the cube.
(b) Find the density of the cube.
(c) Find the volume of the figurine.
(d) Find the density of the figurine.
(e) The shop says both objects are made of the same metal. Use your answers to judge this claim.
questions.a: (a) 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 cm³. (b) 243 / 27 = 9 g/cm³. (c) 70 - 40 = 30 mL = 30 cm³. (d) 81 / 30 = 2.7 g/cm³. (e) The claim is not supported: density does not depend on shape or size, so two objects of the same solid metal would have the same density, but these have 9 g/cm³ and 2.7 g/cm³.
s: (a) Volume of cube 27 cm³
(b) Density of cube 9 g/cm³
(c) Volume of figurine 30 cm³ by displacement
(d) Density of figurine 2.7 g/cm³
(e) Rejects the claim, since the same material has the same density whatever its shape or size

questions.q: Generally, what happens to the density of a substance when it is heated?
questions.a: It decreases.
o: It stays the same, because the mass does not change
It increases, because the particles move faster

questions.q: At which temperature is the density of water the highest?

Assertion (A): Hot air moves up through the cooler air around it.
Reason (R): Hot air is less dense than the cooler air around it.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A substance is heated and none of it escapes. (a) What happens to its mass? (b) What happens to its volume, and so to its density?
questions.a: (a) Its mass does not change. (b) Its particles move apart and spread, so its volume increases; since density = mass / volume, its density decreases.
s: (a) Mass stays the same
(b) Volume increases, so density decreases

questions.q: True or false? 'Increasing the pressure on a liquid changes its density a lot, just as it does for a gas.' Give your verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Liquids are nearly incompressible, so pressure has only a small effect on their density. It is mainly the density of gases that increases a lot with pressure.
s: States the verdict: False
Explains that liquids are nearly incompressible, so pressure changes their density only a little

questions.q: One compartment of an ice tray is filled with water exactly up to its rim and kept in a freezer. When the water has frozen completely, what is most likely to be seen?
questions.a: The ice rises a little above the rim, because water expands as it freezes and the same mass takes up more space.
o: The ice rises a little above the rim, because water expands as it freezes
The ice sits a little below the rim, because solids are denser than liquids
The ice stays exactly level with the rim, because its mass has not changed
The ice stays level with the rim, but its mass has increased

questions.q:
Read these statements about density.
I. A hot air balloon rises because the hot air inside it is less dense than the cooler air outside.
II. Ice floats on water because the same mass of water takes up a larger volume after it freezes.
III. For a gas, increasing the pressure decreases its volume and increases its density.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III

questions.q: A test tube is filled completely with water and closed with a cork through which a narrow glass tube passes; the water stands at a mark in the glass tube. (a) When the test tube is placed in a beaker of hot water at about 70 °C, the water level in the glass tube rises. What does this show about the volume and the density of the water? (b) Predict what happens to the level when the test tube is then moved to a beaker of water at 15 °C, and why.
questions.a: (a) The water's volume has increased while its mass stayed the same, so its density has decreased. (b) The level falls: as the water cools, its particles come closer, its volume decreases and its density increases again.
s: (a) Volume increased with mass unchanged, so density decreased
(b) Predicts the level falls, since cooling decreases the volume and increases the density

questions.q:
In a very cold January, the surface of Dal Lake in Srinagar freezes into a layer of ice. A science team measures the water temperature under the ice: just below the ice, 1 °C; 2 m down, 2 °C; 5 m down, 3 °C; at the bottom (8 m), 4 °C. They also find that a block of the lake ice with a volume of 1000 cm³ has a mass of 917 g.
(a) Find the density of the lake ice.
(b) At which of the measured depths is the water densest? Use the chapter's fact about water.
(c) Using (a), explain why the ice forms a layer on top instead of sinking.
(d) A visitor worries that all the fish in the lake must die each winter once the surface freezes. Using the data, judge whether this worry is justified.
questions.a: (a) 917 / 1000 = 0.917 g/cm³. (b) At the bottom (8 m), where the water is at 4 °C, because water is densest at 4 °C. (c) The ice (0.917 g/cm³) is less dense than liquid water (about 1 g/cm³), because water expands when it freezes, so the ice floats as a layer on top. (d) Not justified. The floating ice forms a layer on top, and the water beneath stays liquid at 1 °C to 4 °C, warm enough for fish and other creatures to survive.
s: (a) Density of ice 0.917 g/cm³
(b) Picks the bottom, at 4 °C, where water is densest
(c) Compares 0.917 with about 1 g/cm³ for water and says the ice floats
(d) Judges the worry not justified: liquid water at 1-4 °C stays below the ice layer for the fish

questions.q:
A fixed mass of 3.6 g of air is kept at room temperature in a cylinder fitted with a movable piston. At first the air occupies 3 L.
(a) Find the density of the air in g/L.
(b) The piston is pushed in until the air occupies 2 L, at the same temperature. Find the new density.
(c) Explain, in terms of particles, why the density changed in (b).
(d) A steel block is squeezed in a press with a large force. Will its density change in the same way? Explain.
(e) The same air is now sealed in a rigid steel bottle of 2 L and warmed. Its mass and its volume both stay the same. Decide whether its density changes, giving a reason.
questions.a: (a) 3.6 / 3 = 1.2 g/L. (b) 3.6 / 2 = 1.8 g/L. (c) The pressure pushes the particles of the gas closer together, so the same mass takes up less volume and the density increases. (d) No. The particles of a solid are already very close to each other, so pressure changes its density only negligibly. (e) Its density does not change: density = mass / volume, and neither the mass nor the volume has changed. Heating usually lowers density only because the volume increases, and the rigid bottle stops that.
s: (a) Density 1.2 g/L
(b) New density 1.8 g/L
(c) Particles pushed closer, smaller volume, greater density
(d) Says a solid's density hardly changes, as its particles are already close
(e) Decides no change, since mass and volume are both unchanged
